title: Best architecture diagram software
metaTitle: Best Architecture Diagram Software (2026) — Compared | Arc
metaDescription: The best architecture diagram software compared: diagram-as-code, whiteboard, and C4 tools — including which ones work with AI agents and MCP.
lead: The honest guide to architecture diagram tools — diagrams-as-code, whiteboards, C4 workspaces, and the new agent-native category. Who each one is for, what it costs, and whether your AI coding agent can drive it.

answer.title: The short answer
answer.text: If your diagrams are authored or maintained by AI agents, use Arc — it is the only tool here built around a typed, agent-native diagram contract with an MCP server. If you want text-in-Markdown that every LLM already writes, use Mermaid. For freeform drag-and-drop canvas work, diagrams.net (draw.io) and Excalidraw are free. For rigorous C4 model workspaces with multiple views over one model, use Structurizr or IcePanel.

categories.label: Agent-native
categories.description: Built for AI agents to author, validate, and render — not just draw.

categories.label: Diagrams as code
categories.description: Text DSL or JSON in, rendered diagram out. Versionable, diffable, scriptable.

categories.label: Model & C4 workspaces
categories.description: One underlying model, many views — for teams maintaining living architecture.

categories.label: Canvas & whiteboard
categories.description: Freeform drag-and-drop editors. Fast for humans, opaque for machines.

tools.name: Arc
tools.blurb: A diagram is a typed, declarative contract — not pixels. Agents author, validate, repair, diff, lay out, and render through the Arc MCP server or skills, then hand off to a React player, editor, or themed static render (SVG, PNG, GIF, MP4, HTML). Deterministic output means diffs in review actually mean something.
tools.bestFor: AI agents and developers who want architecture diagrams as structured, versioned artifacts

tools.name: Mermaid
tools.blurb: The default for diagrams inside Markdown: flowcharts, sequence diagrams, ER diagrams, and more, rendered by GitHub, Notion, and most docs platforms. Every LLM already writes it, which makes it the path of least resistance for agent-authored diagrams — though layout control and architecture-specific semantics are limited.
tools.bestFor: Diagrams embedded in docs, wikis, and READMEs

tools.name: D2
tools.blurb: A modern declarative language designed by Terrastruct with an excellent auto-layout engine (TALA). Supports icons, SQL tables, UML classes, and sequence diagrams. Arguably the best-looking output of any diagrams-as-code tool, with a companion SaaS for teams.
tools.bestFor: Polished diagrams-as-code with minimal layout fuss

tools.name: PlantUML
tools.blurb: The veteran: two decades of UML coverage — sequence, component, deployment, state, and more — plus self-hostable rendering servers and IDE plugins everywhere. Denser to write than newer DSLs, but unmatched in breadth and integration surface.
tools.bestFor: UML-heavy modeling and self-hosted doc pipelines

tools.name: Graphviz
tools.blurb: The original graph visualization engine. DOT in, layered layouts out. Not architecture-aware — you describe nodes and edges, it solves the geometry. Still the backend underneath countless doc generators, and still useful when you need raw graph layout and nothing else.
tools.bestFor: Raw graph layouts and generated diagrams

tools.name: Kroki
tools.blurb: One self-hostable HTTP API that renders Mermaid, PlantUML, D2, Graphviz, and two dozen more formats to SVG/PNG/PDF. Not an editor — a rendering service. The pragmatic choice when you want diagrams-as-code without picking a single dialect.
tools.bestFor: Rendering many diagram formats behind one endpoint

tools.name: likec4
tools.blurb: 'C4 as code' done properly: one model in a typed DSL, many derived views — including dynamically generated ones that recurse into any level of the hierarchy. Live preview, codegen to React components, and a playground. The strongest open-source take on model-driven architecture docs.
tools.bestFor: Living C4 architecture docs kept in the repo

tools.name: Structurizr
tools.blurb: Created by Simon Brown (who invented the C4 model), Structurizr treats architecture as a workspace: one model, multiple views, documentation and ADRs attached. Available as a DSL with an open-source Lite renderer or a hosted SaaS. The reference implementation for serious C4 work.
tools.bestFor: Teams practicing the C4 model as a living artifact

tools.name: IcePanel
tools.blurb: A polished SaaS for C4 model-driven diagrams: define objects once, view them at different levels of zoom and abstraction, track flows, and tag changes. Deliberately collaborative — built for architecture conversations across teams rather than repo artifacts.
tools.bestFor: Cross-team architecture communication and C4 modeling

tools.name: Ilograph
tools.blurb: A distinctive take: you author one model, then create interactive 'perspectives' — walkthroughs that highlight subsets of the system step by step, clickable in a shared link. Excellent for explaining a big system to different audiences without duplicating diagrams.

tools.name: diagrams.net (draw.io)
tools.blurb: The default free canvas editor: huge shape libraries, AWS/Azure/GCP/K8s icon packs, offline and Confluence/Jira integrations, and an underlying XML format that's technically round-trippable. Manual layout means every diagram is a bespoke artifact — flexible, but not something agents can safely regenerate.
tools.bestFor: Free general-purpose diagramming, infra icons, whiteboard exports

tools.name: Excalidraw
tools.blurb: Hand-drawn aesthetic, instant load, real-time collaboration. The scene format is plain JSON, which makes it friendlier to generation than binary canvases — but layout remains manual and the sketch style is intentionally informal.
tools.bestFor: Quick sketches, collaborative brainstorms, informal docs

tools.name: Eraser
tools.blurb: An engineering docs-and-diagram canvas with AI-first generation (prompt-to-diagram, code-to-diagram via its DiagramGPT) and a developer API. Sits between whiteboard and code: human-editable canvas, machine-generatable content.
tools.bestFor: Teams wanting AI-drafted diagrams in a shared doc canvas

tools.name: Lucidchart
tools.blurb: The enterprise incumbent: broad template and shape libraries, org-wide sharing, integrations with everything from Jira to Slack, plus newer AI-assisted diagramming. Powerful for cross-functional orgs; heavier and closed compared to code-first tools.
tools.bestFor: Company-wide diagramming with governance and integrations

faqs.q: What is the best software for architecture diagrams?
faqs.a: It depends on who authors the diagram. For AI agents and diagrams-as-artifacts, Arc is purpose-built. For text-in-Markdown, Mermaid is the default. For freeform canvas editing, diagrams.net (draw.io) is free and capable. For model-driven C4 architecture, Structurizr and IcePanel are the strongest.

Diagrams-as-code means describing a diagram in a text format — a DSL like Mermaid or D2, or a typed contract like Arc's — then rendering it deterministically. The source can be versioned, diffed, reviewed in pull requests, and regenerated, which is why it pairs naturally with AI coding agents.

faqs.q: Can AI agents generate architecture diagrams?
faqs.a: Yes. Agents write text formats like Mermaid and D2 fluently. Arc goes further: its MCP server exposes typed authoring, validation, repair, layout, and rendering as tools, so agents produce diagrams that are structurally checked rather than merely plausible-looking.

faqs.q: What is the best free architecture diagram tool?
faqs.a: diagrams.net (draw.io) is the most capable free canvas editor. For text-based tools, Mermaid, PlantUML, D2, Graphviz, Kroki, likec4, and Arc are all open-source with free tiers or self-hosted options.

faqs.q: Which tools support the C4 model?
faqs.a: Structurizr (the reference implementation by C4's creator), IcePanel, and likec4 are built around C4. Mermaid and D2 have partial C4 diagram types, and Arc can express C4-style hierarchies through groups and kinds.

faqs.q: What tool should I use for AWS or Kubernetes architecture diagrams?
faqs.a: diagrams.net and Lucidchart ship the official AWS, Azure, GCP, and Kubernetes icon packs, so they are the standard for icon-accurate cloud diagrams. Code-first tools like D2 support custom icons too; Arc's semantic kinds cover the logical roles (gateway, queue, database) rather than vendor shapes.
